## 1. Intro and framework
- Classic "design a URL shortener": everybody's first SD question
- Slower pace; teaches concepts taken for granted elsewhere
  - For people new to SD or dusting off cobwebs
- Framework (same in every interview)
  1. Requirements: functional (core features) + non-functional (qualities: scale, durability, fault tolerance)
  2. Core entities: what is persisted and exchanged; like table/collection names
  3. API: user-facing contract between client and backend
  4. Data flow: skipped; only for infra-heavy questions (rate limiter, message queue)
  5. High-level design: boxes and arrows; goal = satisfy functional requirements
     - Simple; won't scale or do anything fancy yet
  6. Deep dives: go one by one through NFRs and evolve the design
- End state: all FRs and NFRs met; you feel like you passed

## 2. Functional requirements
- Identify the top 2–3 features you have time to design in 35–45 min
- Unknown system? Pepper the interviewer with questions
- What a URL shortener is
  - Converts long URLs into short ones
  - Short URL redirects to the original
- Write them as "users should be able to…"
  1. Users can create a short URL from a long (original) URL
     - Optionally support a custom alias (e.g. `/evan`, if not already taken)
     - Optionally support an expiration time
       - E.g. valid only for a conference week
       - After expiry: an error saying it expired
  2. Users can be redirected to the original URL from the short URL
- Custom alias and expiration: "a little flavor often added"; he has candidates address them

## 3. Non-functional requirements
- Qualities, not features: the "-ilities"
  - Scalability, latency, durability, security, fault tolerance, compliance, CAP
- Hard for junior candidates
  - Keep a list handy; go one by one
  - Pick the ones uniquely interesting and relevant to this system
- Write them as "the system should…"
- 1. Low latency on redirects, ~200 ms
  - In context: not just "low latency", specifically on redirects
  - Quantified: 200 ms is what humans perceive as real time
    - Under 200 ms you wouldn't notice; a snap of a finger
- 2. Scale to 100M DAU and 1B URLs
  - Ask the interviewer about scale; they may ask you to estimate or just tell you
  - He'd tell the candidate: 100M DAU, ~1B URLs shortened over all time
- 3. Ensure uniqueness of short codes
  - "A little handwavy" whether it's an NFR, but too important to skip
  - No collisions, so nobody lands on an unexpected site
- 4. CAP: high availability, eventual consistency for URL shortening
  - CAP: of consistency, availability, partition tolerance, only two
  - Partition tolerance is a given in distributed systems
    - Multiple DB instances, horizontally scaled servers
  - So: consistency or availability?
  - Ask: do I need strong read-after-write consistency?
    - Must every read see the latest write, or the system breaks?
  - Needs it: banking, ticket booking
    - Last Taylor Swift ticket in Germany; someone in America reads stale "available"
    - Both book; both show up fighting for the same seat; fatal
    - Low-float stock trade must be seen everywhere before you buy or sell
  - URL shortener doesn't
    - Sharing a link takes time; that's time to become consistent
    - Someone wicked quick: route them to the same original node
    - Or show "still saving, try again in a minute"; the world doesn't end

## 4. On up-front estimation
- Many guides say do back-of-envelope estimation now
- Fine to do, but he finds it useless up front, as an interviewer
  - Candidates do storage/latency math, then say "so it's a big distributed system"
  - "We kind of knew that already"
  - It doesn't change the design
- Instead, tell the interviewer
  - "I'd rather not do math up front; I'll do it in HLD or deep dives if I need it for a decision"
- Do math when the result directly informs a decision

## 5. Core entities
- The tables your system persists and exchanges via APIs
- Just list them; full data model later
  - Say so proactively: "I'll be explicit about fields in the HLD"
- Entities: original URL, short URL, user
- This system is simple enough to do the data model now
  - Normally too early, before thinking through the API

## 6. API
- Go methodically: usually one FR maps to one endpoint
  - Not always: sometimes 2–3 endpoints, sometimes none

```text
// shorten a URL (FR 1)
POST /urls -> shortUrl
{
  originalUrl,
  alias?,
  expirationTime?
}

// redirect (FR 2)
GET /{shortUrl} -> 302 redirect to originalUrl
```

- REST notes
  - Verbs: POST create, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE delete, GET fetch
  - Paths: typically plural nouns
  - He doesn't care much; "silly semantics", easy to fix
  - But at lower levels some interviewers are "RESTful API zealots"; be aware
- Redirect works because GET hits our server with the short code
- Check: an endpoint for each FR

## 7. HLD: shorten flow
- Method: start from each API, draw what's needed to satisfy it
  - Same as going FR by FR, but clearer on data flow and inputs/outputs
- Classic client -> primary server -> database
- Shorten flow
  1. Client POSTs `/urls`
  2. Primary server creates short code: a black box for now
  3. Save to DB, return short URL
- Data model: combine short and long into one table (simple case)

```text
URL table
- shortUrl / customAlias (PK)
- longUrl
- expirationTime?
- creationTime
- userId (FK)

User table
- userId
- ... (email, password hash, salt: auxiliary)
```

- Many candidates get distracted by user-table details; focus on core

## 8. HLD: redirect flow, 301 vs 302
- Redirect flow
  1. Client GETs `/{shortUrl}`
  2. Server looks up long URL by short URL (the PK)
  3. Returns the long URL with a 302 redirect
  4. Browser navigates automatically
- 301 = permanent
  - Browsers, "DNS servers potentially" can cache it
  - Future requests may never reach our service
- 302 = temporary
  - "Never cached"; always comes to us first
- Trade-off
  - 302 if analytics: every click hits the server, so you can log it
  - 301 if worried about compute cost: caches elsewhere absorb traffic
- His choice: 302, even at extra server cost
  - Internally you still want to see traffic
  - If requests drop off a cliff, you know something broke, probably client-side
  - 301 loses that visibility
  - "This is the argument I'd make in an interview"

## 9. HLD: custom alias and expiration
- He re-checks the FRs and notices two sub-features not covered
- Custom alias
  - Look up in DB: does the alias exist?
  - If not, insert a row with short URL = alias, return it
- Expiration
  - Store it in the row
  - On redirect: if now > expirationTime, return an error, not a 302

## 10. Deep dive: unique short codes
- Starts out of order with uniqueness: the core he black-boxed
  - Intentional: candidates go too deep too early, then run out of time
  - Say "I'm black-boxing this, I'll come back"
- Goals for code generation: fast, unique, short (5–7 characters)
- Build from simple to complex

### 10.1 Prefix of the long URL
- Take the first 5–7 characters
- Obviously bad: tons of URLs share a prefix (twitter.com, facebook.com)
- One short to many long: can't tell which one; don't do it

### 10.2 Random number + base62
- Much better
- Must cover at least 1B values; 10^9 = 10 characters, too long
  - More than 1B to reduce collisions: 11, 12, 13 characters
- Base62 encoding
  - Digits 0–9, then A–Z, then a–z
  - 10 = A, 11 = B; each character encodes 62 options vs 10
- Length 6: 62^6 ≈ 56 billion combinations
- Collision risk: birthday paradox
  - 23 people: over 50% chance two share a birthday, despite 365 days
  - Same formula: 1B random picks from 56B
  - His estimate: ~880K collisions
  - Not needed in an interview; he computed it out of interest
- Fix: check for collision first
  - Read the DB for the code; write only if it doesn't exist
  - An extra read; not a big deal

### 10.3 Hash the long URL
- Common online and among candidates
- `md5(longUrl)` (or murmur, SHA-256) -> base62 -> take first 6
- Avalanche effect: one bit changes the whole hash
- So output is just as random as option 2
  - Same 56B space, exactly the same collision chance
  - Same fix: check the DB first

### 10.4 Counter + base62 (his preference)
- First URL gets 1, second 2, and so on; base62 encode
- Never collides: strictly increasing
- Fast to grab, unique, short
- Flaw: predictability is bad for security
  - Competitors learn how many URLs you have
  - Anyone can scrape all long URLs by incrementing
  - Options
    - Product decision: warn "don't shorten private URLs"
    - Rate limiting to stop scraping
    - Bijective function: one-to-one mapping that obfuscates
      - E.g. Sqids (sqids.org)
      - Number in, bit.ly-looking base62 string out
      - "You don't need to know this; they'd probably be impressed"
- No DB read needed: every code is unique
- "Counter on a single server?" Handled in scale section
- Options 2 and 3 pass if you call out the collision check
- Option 4 he likes; small differences overall

## 11. Deep dive: low-latency redirects
- Expensive part: the DB lookup
- No index: scan 1B rows; prohibitively expensive
- Index
  - Primary key enforces uniqueness and auto-builds an index
  - Index often kept in memory; points to location on disk
  - Seek straight to the row instead of scanning
  - Postgres uses a B-tree: self-balancing, O(log n), often faster with optimizations
  - Optional extra hash index: O(1)
    - Not needed; B-trees are well optimized for equality lookups
- Still goes to disk; SSDs are fast, but memory is faster
- Cache (Redis, Memcached)
  - Just another server; use its RAM
  - Read-through: on miss, read DB, populate cache, return
  - LRU eviction: hot URLs stay; old URLs nobody uses get evicted
  - Key = short code, value = long URL; O(1) on hit
- CDN (optional; he'd stop at the cache)
  - Edge servers worldwide; e.g. service in California, user in China
  - Cache redirect responses at the edge
  - Same issue as 301: requests never reach the primary server
  - Care about health visibility and analytics? No CDN
  - Don't care? CDN, and might as well use 301
- "There's no right or wrong answer; it's trade-offs"

## 12. Deep dive: scale
- Walk left to right through components looking for bottlenecks
- Primary server math (use exponents)
  - 100M DAU, ~1 redirect each = 10^8 per day
  - ~10^5 seconds per day
  - 10^8 / 10^5 = 10^3 = 1,000 RPS average
  - Peaks ×10 to ×100: 10K–100K RPS
- Intuition: a t3.medium EC2 handles ~1,000 concurrent requests
  - "Intentionally handwavy"; depends on CPU, memory, payload, bandwidth
- Vertical scaling: bigger box; more expensive
- Horizontal scaling: more boxes; most common in SD; chosen
- Read-heavy
  - Redirects ~100K/s peak; creates maybe 1/1000 of that, ~1 per second
- Split into microservices
  - Read service (redirects), write service (create)
  - API gateway as entry point; routes by endpoint
  - Scale read service wide, write service small
  - Caveat: little code in each; two services to maintain; "probably overkill"
    - Keeping one service is a valid option too
- Autoscaling in modern cloud (GCP, AWS, Azure)
  - E.g. above 75% memory/CPU add a box; below 20% remove one
  - A load balancer in front, round robin or configured
- Counter problem with many write servers
  - Each in-memory counter starts at 0: duplicate codes
  - Move to a global counter, e.g. Redis
    - `INCR`; single-threaded so no concurrency issues; in memory, fast
  - Adds a network hop per create
  - Trick: on start, a server grabs the next 1,000 counts and uses them locally
    - Server dies: those counts are lost forever; fine
    - "Up to 3.5 trillion" before needing a 7th character
- Database math
  - Short code 8 B, long URL 100 B, creation time 8 B, alias up to 100 B, expiration 8 B
  - ~232 B; round up to 500 B for extra fields
  - 500 B × 1B rows = 500 GB
  - Not a lot; "modern SSDs are in the hundreds of terabytes"
  - Single DB instance is fine
  - Read throughput: most reads hit Redis; DB is "chilling"
  - If needed: shard by short URL (e.g. short URL mod 3)
  - Math proved we don't need it

## 13. Deep dive: high availability
- Autoscaling and horizontal scaling already give most of it
- Redis cache down: "honestly I don't care"
  - Read-through; reload from DB; slow for a bit
- Global counter down: a problem
  - Redis high-availability mode: redundancy
  - Periodically snapshot the count to disk
- Database
  - A single replica: promote if primary dies
  - Hourly snapshots to S3 (cheap blob storage); restore from there

## 14. Close
- Check back against requirements
  - FRs met in HLD; NFRs met in deep dives
- "I know I've crushed it because we agreed on requirements and I satisfied them"

- Text version, assembled from the talk
  - FR: create short URL (optional alias, optional expiration); redirect
  - NFR: redirects ~200 ms; 100M DAU, 1B URLs; unique codes; HA, eventual consistency
  - Entities: original URL, short URL, user
  - Code options: prefix (bad); random + base62 (62^6 = 56B, collisions, check first); hash (same); counter + base62 (predictable; bijective function, sqids.org)

```text
                         Redis (read-through LRU; key shortCode -> longUrl)
                           |
client --302-- API gateway -- Read Service --- Database (URL table, ~500 GB)
                         \-- Write Service --/
                                 |
                          Global Counter (INCR)
10^8 / 10^5 = 10^3 = 1,000 rps; peaks 10K–100K rps
```
